description: remote sensing & GIS engineering students from Algeria, working with Python, QGIS, satellite imagery and ML to build a NASA data-driven solution.
summary:
AgroShift is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers in Finney County, Kansas choose their next crop rotation. Western Kansas farmers face a falling Ogallala aquifer (median decline of 2.6 ft/year), erosion from bare fallow, and nutrient depletion, and a crop that helps the soil in one place can use too much water or fail on the market.

For any parcel, we simulate the farmer’s current rotation plus three alternatives (no fallow, wheat–sorghum–soybean, and three-year alfalfa). A Random Forest model, trained on 2018–2024 satellite history for 3,522 one-kilometer cells (NASA ECOSTRESS, OpenET evapotranspiration, NDVI, soil moisture, USDA crop maps), predicts water use, vigor and bare-soil months. Each rotation is scored against the current one on five criteria: water, income, soil, erosion and resilience. Farmers set their own priorities with simple sliders, so the ranking updates live, and the tool shows uncertainty and aquifer alerts.

It keeps the human in the loop: it supports the decision and does not replace the farmer or agronomist.
details:
Project Details

What it does and how it works
AgroShift lets a farmer draw their field on a map and enter priorities from 1 to 9 for five criteria: water, income, soil, erosion and resilience. The tool then compares four rotations: the current wheat–sorghum–fallow, plus three alternatives (wheat–sorghum without fallow, wheat–sorghum–soybean, and three-year alfalfa followed by wheat). A Random Forest model, trained on 2018–2024 satellite history for 3,522 one-kilometer cells, predicts water use, crop vigor and bare-soil months for each rotation. Each rotation is scored relative to the farmer’s current one (a ±30% change earns the full score) and ranked using weights computed by the AHP method from the farmer’s sliders. Results update live. The site also shows model uncertainty, an alert against alfalfa where the local water table falls faster than 2 ft/year, a 3-day irrigation advice, and live NASA GIBS satellite layers.

Benefits and intended impact
Farmers see the trade-off between water, profit and soil, instead of a single yield ranking. A profit-only ranking picks alfalfa in 99% of cells but uses about 25% more water; our tool makes that visible and shows soybean as a good water-saving option. The intended impact is better rotation decisions that reduce bare fallow, protect the Ogallala aquifer and keep farms economically viable. The tool supports the decision and does not replace the farmer or the agronomist.

Tools and technologies
Google Earth Engine (data extraction), Python (pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, joblib), SQLite, Flask, Streamlit and Folium, Leaflet, Chart.js, jsPDF, HTML/JavaScript (English, French and Arabic interface), Jupyter and Visual Studio Code. Data: NASA SMAP (soil moisture), NASA GPM (rainfall), Landsat and MODIS (vegetation indices such as NDVI and NDMI), NASA ECOSTRESS surface temperature, OpenET evapotranspiration, USDA Cropland Data Layer (2012–2024), USDA QuickStats yields and prices, LANDFIRE, KGS/USGS well measurements (1934–2026), Open-Meteo/ERA5 and NASA GIBS (MODIS, IMERG). We used AI assistants (Claude and Gemini) to help write and review code; the team chose and verified the data, criteria and validation.

What is creative
Instead of ranking crops by yield, we compare rotations against the farmer’s own current practice and let the farmer set priorities with simple sliders, while AHP works invisibly in the background. We also linked the crop decision to the aquifer, using interpolated well trends and live USGS data.

Factors we considered
Spatial validation on unseen 10 km blocks (R² of 0.46 to 0.61, better than a simple baseline of 0.29 to 0.30). Data quality control (corrected CDL rounding, removed aberrant temperatures, flagged disagreement between two ET sources). Honest limits: soil scores are expert assumptions, alfalfa yield is a default value, income is gross revenue without costs, and the model is trained on Finney County only, so results elsewhere are a demonstration.
